steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on generating pseudo scene flow labels automatically for LiDAR point clouds in autonomous driving. Explain why current learning-based scene flow methods struggle on real data, outline our box-based auto-labelling and augmentation idea, and end with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. 3D scene flow: definition, applications, learning-based methods, reliance on synthetic data
2. Synthetic-to-real gap and the cost of real labels
3. Our approach: rigid-motion-based auto-labelling with 3D boxes
4. Data augmentation for diverse motion patterns, results
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Scene flow
- per-point motion field from consecutive point cloud frames
- applications: motion prediction, anomaly motion detection, 3D object detection, dynamic point cloud accumulation
- deep learning on point clouds -> many learning-based methods
- some SOTA methods: average EPE3D down to a few centimetres on KITTI Scene Flow (stereoKITTI)
- scarce labels -> heavy reliance on synthetic data, FlyingThings3D (FT3D)

2. Gap to real world
- PV-RAFT: EPE3D 0.056m on stereoKITTI, but > 10m on Argoverse
- Jin et al.: GTA-SF synthetic dataset simulating LiDAR scans; teacher-student domain adaptation; still poor on real LiDAR (ideal sensor models, little scene variety)
- ideally learn from real sensor data, but labelling per-point 3D motion extremely costly
- -> unsupervised / self-supervised methods; reasonable accuracy, still behind supervised

3. Our approach
- three challenges: synthetic data generalizes poorly, scarce real labels, poor performance of networks on real LiDAR
- inspired by rigid motion assumptions in RigidFlow and RSF
- 3D anchor boxes segment objects; box attributes: position, size, rotation, translation, motion status, normal vector
- constrained losses on box parameters + inter-frame association -> optimize boxes -> combine with source cloud -> realistic target cloud
- one-to-one correspondence source/target -> pseudo 3D scene flow labels (Fig. 1)

4. Augmentation
- Gaussian noise on box attributes simulates rotations, translations, motion status of ego vehicle and surroundings
- many labels with diverse, realistic motions -> better generalization
- SOTA across various models and datasets (Fig. 2)

5. Contributions
- auto-labelling framework for pseudo-labels; addresses label scarcity
- universal 3D box optimization with multiple motion attributes; plug-and-play augmentation module (global-local motions, motion status)
- SOTA on KITTI, nuScenes, Argoverse LiDAR; beats supervised and unsupervised methods without synthetic data or manual labels

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
3D scene flow estimation means deducing the per-point motion field from consecutive frames of point clouds. It is important for many applications, such as motion prediction, anomaly motion detection, 3D object detection, and dynamic point cloud accumulation. As deep learning on point clouds has advanced, many works have developed learning-based methods to estimate per-point motion from 3D point clouds. Some state-of-the-art methods have brought the average 3D EndPoint Error (EPE3D) down to a few centimetres on the KITTI Scene Flow dataset (stereoKITTI). But because scene flow labels are scarce, these methods depend heavily on synthetic datasets like FlyingThings3D (FT3D) for training the network.

For example, on the stereoKITTI dataset, PV-RAFT has an average EPE3D of only 0.056m. But on the Argoverse dataset, its EPE3D is more than 10m, which is surprising. So learning 3D scene flow on a synthetic dataset leaves a big gap to real-world use. Recently Jin et al. introduced a new synthetic dataset, GTA-SF, which simulates LiDAR scans for autonomous driving. They also proposed a teacher-student domain adaptation framework to reduce the gap between synthetic and real datasets, and this improves the 3D scene flow estimation performance somewhat. However, the performance on real-world LiDAR data is still poor, because the sensor models are ideal and there is not much variety in the scenes. Ideally, in autonomous driving the models should learn from real sensor data. But labelling the 3D motion vector of each point for the 3D scene flow task is extremely expensive. Because of this many works have moved to unsupervised or self-supervised learning of 3D scene flow. These methods get reasonable accuracy, but they are still behind supervised methods, which shows that real sensor data and the matching 3D scene flow labels are important.

- Our approach:
  - three challenges: poor generalization of synthetic data, scarce real labels, poor performance on real LiDAR
  - inspired by rigid motion in RigidFlow and RSF (Fig. 1)
  - 3D anchor boxes; attributes: position, size, rotation, translation, motion status, normal vector
  - constrained losses + inter-frame association -> optimize boxes -> realistic target point cloud
  - one-to-one correspondence -> pseudo 3D scene flow labels
- Augmentation:
  - Gaussian noise on box attributes, ego vehicle + surroundings
  - diverse realistic motions, better generalization
  - SOTA across models and datasets (Fig. 2)
- Contributions:
  - auto-labelling framework
  - box optimization + plug-and-play augmentation module
  - SOTA on KITTI, nuScenes, Argoverse without synthetic data or manual labels

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
3D scene flow estimation means deducing the per-point motion field from consecutive frames of point clouds. It is important for many applications, such as motion prediction, anomaly motion detection, 3D object detection, and dynamic point cloud accumulation. As deep learning on point clouds has advanced, many works have developed learning-based methods to estimate per-point motion from 3D point clouds. Some state-of-the-art methods have brought the average 3D EndPoint Error (EPE3D) down to a few centimetres on the KITTI Scene Flow dataset (stereoKITTI). But because scene flow labels are scarce, these methods depend heavily on synthetic datasets like FlyingThings3D (FT3D) for training the network.

For example, on the stereoKITTI dataset, PV-RAFT has an average EPE3D of only 0.056m. But on the Argoverse dataset, its EPE3D is more than 10m, which is surprising. So learning 3D scene flow on a synthetic dataset leaves a big gap to real-world use. Recently Jin et al. introduced a new synthetic dataset, GTA-SF, which simulates LiDAR scans for autonomous driving. They also proposed a teacher-student domain adaptation framework to reduce the gap between synthetic and real datasets, and this improves the 3D scene flow estimation performance somewhat. However, the performance on real-world LiDAR data is still poor, because the sensor models are ideal and there is not much variety in the scenes. Ideally, in autonomous driving the models should learn from real sensor data. But labelling the 3D motion vector of each point for the 3D scene flow task is extremely expensive. Because of this many works have moved to unsupervised or self-supervised learning of 3D scene flow. These methods get reasonable accuracy, but they are still behind supervised methods, which shows that real sensor data and the matching 3D scene flow labels are important.

In this work we address three key challenges in autonomous driving: synthetic datasets that still generalize poorly to real-world scenarios, scarce scene flow labels in real driving scenes, and the poor performance of existing 3D scene flow estimation networks on real LiDAR data. We were inspired by the rigid motion assumptions in RigidFlow and RSF, and we propose a new scene flow auto-labelling approach that uses the rigid motion that is common in autonomous driving scenarios (Fig. 1). Specifically, we use 3D anchor boxes to segment 3D objects in point clouds. Each object-level box has attributes for position and size, and also rotation, translation, motion status, and normal vector. We use constrained loss functions for the box parameters and inter-frame association to optimize the box attributes, and then we combine these parameters with the source point cloud to make a realistic target point cloud. The important thing is that the generated target point cloud has a one-to-one correspondence with the source point cloud, so pseudo 3D scene flow labels can be generated efficiently.

To get a more diverse range of motion patterns, we also introduce a new data augmentation strategy for 3D scene flow auto-labelling. Using the attributes of each box, we add Gaussian noise to them to simulate the rotations, translations, and motion status of the ego vehicle and the surrounding environment. This gives us many 3D scene flow labels with diverse motions that are close to real-world scenarios. This gives the neural network a lot of real training data and improves the generalization of learning-based methods significantly. Our experiments show that our pseudo-label generation strategy gets state-of-the-art scene flow estimation results consistently across different models and datasets (Fig. 2).

Our contributions are:

- We propose a new framework for automatically labelling 3D scene flow pseudo-labels. It improves the accuracy of current scene flow estimation models a lot and addresses the scarcity of 3D flow labels in autonomous driving.

- We propose a universal 3D box optimization method with multiple motion attributes. On top of this we introduce a plug-and-play 3D scene flow augmentation module with global-local motions and motion status. It allows flexible adjustment of ego-motion and dynamic environments and sets a new benchmark for scene flow data augmentation.

- Our method gets state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI, nuScenes, and Argoverse LiDAR datasets. It surpasses all supervised and unsupervised methods without needing any synthesising data or manual scene flow labels.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
3D scene flow estimation, which deduces the per-point motion field from consecutive frames of point clouds, plays a critical role in various applications, including motion prediction [1,2], anomaly motion detection [3], 3D object detection [4,5], and dynamic point cloud accumulation [6]. With the advance of deep learning on point clouds [7,8], many works [9,10,11,12,13,14,15] have developed learning-based methods to estimate per-point motion from 3D point clouds. Some state-of-the-art methods [12,14,15] have reduced the average 3D EndPoint Error (EPE3D) to a few centimetres on the KITTI Scene Flow dataset (stereoKITTI) [16,17]. However, due to the scarcity of scene flow labels, these methods rely heavily on synthetic datasets such as FlyingThings3D (FT3D) [18] for network training.

When evaluated on the stereoKITTI dataset [16,17], PV-RAFT [19] shows an average EPE3D of just 0.056m. However, on the Argoverse dataset [20], its EPE3D surprisingly exceeds 10m [21]. Learning 3D scene flow on a synthetic dataset [18] therefore leaves a large gap to real-world application. Jin et al. [13] recently introduced a new synthetic dataset, GTA-SF, which simulates LiDAR scans for autonomous driving, and proposed a teacher-student domain adaptation framework that reduces the gap between synthetic and real datasets and improves 3D scene flow estimation to some extent. Their performance on real-world LiDAR data nevertheless remains poor, because of ideal sensor models and a lack of scene variety. Ideally, models in the autonomous driving field should learn from real sensor data, but labelling the 3D motion vector of each point is extremely costly. This has driven many works [22,23,12,24,9,25] towards unsupervised or self-supervised learning of 3D scene flow. Although these methods achieve reasonable accuracy, they still lag behind supervised methods, which highlights the importance of real sensor data and corresponding 3D scene flow labels.

In this work, we address three key challenges in autonomous driving: the reliance on synthetic datasets that still generalize poorly to real-world scenarios, the scarcity of scene flow labels in actual driving scenes, and the poor performance of existing 3D scene flow estimation networks on real LiDAR data. Inspired by the rigid motion assumptions in RigidFlow [24] and RSF [27], we propose a novel scene flow auto-labelling approach that exploits the rigid motion prevalent in autonomous driving scenarios (Fig. 1). Specifically, we use 3D anchor boxes to segment 3D objects in point clouds. Each object-level box has not only position and size attributes but also rotation, translation, motion status, and normal vector attributes. Using constrained loss functions for the box parameters and inter-frame association, we optimize the box attributes and then combine these parameters with the source point cloud to produce a realistic target point cloud. Importantly, the generated target point cloud keeps a one-to-one correspondence with the source point cloud, which allows pseudo 3D scene flow labels to be generated efficiently.

To capture a more diverse range of motion patterns, we introduce a novel data augmentation strategy for 3D scene flow auto-labelling. Using the attributes of each box, we simulate the rotations, translations, and motion status of both the ego vehicle and the surrounding environment by adding Gaussian noise to these attributes. As a result, we obtain numerous 3D scene flow labels with diverse motions that closely resemble real-world scenarios, which provides the neural network with rich real training data and significantly improves the generalization of learning-based methods. Experimental results show that our pseudo-label generation strategy consistently achieves state-of-the-art scene flow estimation results across various models [10,14,15] and datasets [16,20,26] (Fig. 2).

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- We propose a new framework for automatically labelling 3D scene flow pseudo-labels, which significantly improves the accuracy of current scene flow estimation models and effectively addresses the scarcity of 3D flow labels in autonomous driving.

- We propose a universal 3D box optimization method with multiple motion attributes, and on top of it a plug-and-play 3D scene flow augmentation module with global-local motions and motion status. This allows flexible adjustment of ego-motion and dynamic environments, setting a new benchmark for scene flow data augmentation.

- Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI, nuScenes, and Argoverse LiDAR datasets. Our approach surpasses all supervised and unsupervised methods without requiring any synthesising data or manual scene flow labels.
